title: Which cuts break a friend network?
hook: Cut the closest friendships or the loosest ones. Which leaves the network in pieces?

knows: strong ties sit inside groups and weak ties between them
doesNotKnow: that removing the weakest links first shatters a network far faster than removing the strongest first

misconception: Cutting the strongest, closest relationships does the most damage to a network.
objective: The learner can explain that links with few shared friends are mostly the bridges between groups, so cutting them first breaks a network into its groups, while cutting close ties inside groups leaves it in one piece.

claims.text: In the stage's networks, cutting the 20% of links with the least overlap leaves a largest group of 10 to 20 of the 60 people; cutting the 20% with the most overlap leaves all 60 in one piece.
claims.source: Builder's own code (makeNet/stateAt in Demo.tsx), re-run in node 2026-10-14 via a transpile-only harness. Model as briefed: 6 groups of 10, each within-group pair linked with probability 0.5, plus 12 distinct random between-group links, mulberry32(seed). Links with equal overlap are cut in a seeded random order (tie key stream mulberry32(seed + 1000)). Cut count = round(share × links). Seed list, chosen by rule: the first five seeds from 1 whose network starts in one piece, i.e. 1, 3, 5, 6, 7 (seeds 2 and 4 skipped because they start disconnected, largest group 50 and 59). The spec's rule also asks that the weak-first 20% cut leaves 30 or fewer; all five meet it, so no seed was skipped for its result. Pinned figures, largest group at 0/10/20/30/40% cut, weakest first | strongest first: seed 1 (149 links) 60/28/10/10/10 | 60/60/60/59/59; seed 3 (134) 60/56/20/10/10 | 60/60/60/57/55; seed 5 (151) 60/59/10/10/10 | 60/60/60/59/58; seed 6 (148) 60/30/10/10/9 | 60/60/60/58/58; seed 7 (131) 60/40/10/10/9 | 60/60/60/59/56. Context over seeds 1–500 with the same code: 450 start in one piece; weak-first 20% median 10, 90th percentile 20, maximum 48, 433 of 450 at 30 or fewer; strong-first 20% never below 51. The brief's seed-33 figures came from another generator and are not quoted. · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: Own re-implementation (mulberry32, overlap, seeded tie keys): seeds 1, 3, 5, 6, 7 are the first five that start in one piece; weakest-first 20% leaves 10, 20, 10, 10, 10; strongest-first 20% leaves 60 in all five. Note (non-blocking): the reveal quotes the learner's level when it is 30% or 40% (e.g. seed 3 strongest-first 40% leaves 55); those figures are computed and correct but not in any claim. | v4 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, learner r8 / W-307, phone fit): reveal paragraph 1 reworded ('Cutting the 27 loosest first left a largest group of 20, with 10 of the 12 bridges among them.'); the Seen row now reads 'weakest first 20, 10 of 12 bridges cut' (no 'of 60'). Numbers unchanged. Unverified because the text changed. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own run: seed rule skips 2 (largest 50) and 4 (59), giving SEEDS 1, 3, 5, 6, 7. Weakest-first 20% (26-30 links) leaves largest groups 10, 20, 10, 10, 10; strongest-first 20% leaves 60 in all five. So '10 to 20' and 'all 60' hold for every network the learner can reach with New network.

claims.text: Link strength = share of friends in common (stage rule; the model's neighbourhood overlap: shared friends divided by friends of either end, not counting each other).
claims.source: Easley and Kleinberg (2010) ch. 3 (strong and weak ties; neighbourhood overlap). overlap in makeNet, Demo.tsx; a link whose ends have no other friends gets overlap 0. · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: The lesson's definition (stage rule text) matches makeNet(): shared neighbours / union of neighbours excluding the two ends. E&K ch. 3 neighbourhood overlap from my knowledge; not opened. | v4 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, learner r8 / W-307, phone fit): stage rule shortened from 'share of friends the two have in common' to 'share of friends in common' so it fits one line. Definition unchanged. Unverified because the text changed. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Verified as the stage's stated rule, on the code: overlap = shared / (deg a + deg b - shared - 2), i.e. shared friends over friends of either end not counting each other; the stage line reads 'Link strength = share of friends in common.' The attribution of this measure to the literature (neighbourhood overlap) is in the source field only; it was not opened and is not the basis of this verdict.

claims.text: Cutting the 20% weakest links first cuts 12 of the 12 between-group links in networks 1, 3, 4 and 5 (seeds 1, 5, 6, 7) and 10 of 12 in network 2 (seed 3); cutting the strongest 20% first cuts none.
claims.source: stateAt(...).bridgesCut in Demo.tsx, builder re-run 2026-10-14, seeds and tie rule as in c1. In the weak-first order the last between-group link sits at rank 30 (seed 1, of 149), 30 (seed 3, of 134; 27 are cut at 20%), 29 (seed 5), 22 (seed 6) and 25 (seed 7). · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: Own run: bridges cut at 20% weakest-first 12, 10, 12, 12, 12 for seeds 1, 3, 5, 6, 7; strongest-first 0 in all. | v4 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, learner r8 / W-307, phone fit): the reveal now says '10 of the 12 bridges' (was '10 of the 12 links between groups'), the stage's own word ('bridges cut'). Unverified because the text changed. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own run at 20%: weakest-first cuts 12/12 bridges in seeds 1, 5, 6, 7 (networks 1, 3, 4, 5) and 10/12 in seed 3 (network 2); strongest-first cuts 0 in all five.

claims.text: In the stage's networks, the links between groups all have few shared friends, so cutting the weakest links first removes them and breaks the network apart; close ties sit inside groups, and the groups hold together without them.
claims.source: Easley and Kleinberg (2010) ch. 3 (local bridges have neighbourhood overlap 0; weak ties as bridges between tightly knit groups); illustrated on the stage by c1 and c3. · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: DISPUTED (direction). Own run of the lesson's networks: bridges almost all have overlap 0 (the max is 0.13), but most links with few shared friends are inside groups: links with overlap 0 are 18/28/29/24/27 in seeds 1/3/5/6/7, of which only 10/10/12/12/12 are bridges, and the weakest 20% (26-30 links) holds 9-12 bridges. So 'a link with few shared friends usually runs between groups' is false here; the converse is true. Fix (builder, reveal and claim): 'Links between groups almost always have few shared friends, so cutting the weakest links first removes them and breaks the network apart. Close ties sit inside groups, and the groups hold together without them.' | Builder revision v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): reworded per fact-check pass 23 (direction: it is the between-group links that have few shared friends, not the reverse). The sentence now rests only on the stage's five networks, not on Easley and Kleinberg ch. 3, which no checker has opened. Evidence: the fact-checker's own run (pass 23) found between-group links have overlap 0 in almost all cases (max 0.13), and c3 gives 12, 10, 12, 12, 12 of 12 between-group links cut by the weakest-first 20% (seeds 1, 3, 5, 6, 7). c1 shows the strongest-first 20% leaves all 60 in one piece. Reveal text: 'Here the links between groups all have few shared friends, so cutting the weakest first removes them and breaks the network apart. Close ties sit inside groups, and the groups hold together without them.' | FC pass 24 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Own replay (fc24/weak.mjs, own mulberry32 copy, own overlap and union-find): seeds 1, 3, 5, 6, 7 (first five connected). Between-group links' overlap max 0.13, 0.09, 0, 0, 0 (in-group mean 0.28-0.32). Weakest-first 20% cuts 12, 10, 12, 12, 12 of 12 bridges and leaves largest 10, 20, 10, 10, 10; strongest-first 20% cuts 0 bridges (min overlap cut 0.40-0.50, all inside groups) and leaves 60 of 60 in every network. The v2 wording now runs in the right direction (between-group links have few shared friends) and rests on the stage's own networks only; no unopened source is relied on. In network 2 'removes them' is 10 of 12, which the reveal's first paragraph states. | v4 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, learner r8 / W-307, phone fit): reveal sentence now says 'cutting the weakest links first' (was 'cutting the weakest first'), the same words as this claim. Unverified because the reveal text changed. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own run: bridge overlaps are at most 0.125 (seed 1), 0.091 (seed 3) and 0 in seeds 5, 6, 7, the bottom of the overlap range, so weakest-first reaches them within 20%; strongest-first removes only within-group links and every network stays in one piece at 20% (60 of 60). Scoped 'in the stage's networks', which is what was checked. Note: some within-group links also have overlap 0 (12-18 per network), so 'weak' is not a perfect bridge detector, but the claim does not say it is.

claims.text: The stage's network: 60 people in 6 friend groups of 10, with 12 links between groups.
claims.source: The lesson's model (brief weak-links-hold-it-together, company/domains/briefs/probability.chance.md, Course: NCM); a toy model, not data about a real network. · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: GROUPS 6 x SIZE 10, BRIDGES 12 distinct between-group links in makeNet(); predict text '60 people, 6 friend groups'.

recall.question: A company wants to keep its teams talking. Which relationships, if lost, would split it into isolated teams fastest?
options: The closest friendships inside each team
The loose acquaintances between teams who share few contacts
It makes no difference which go
recall.why: Links with few shared contacts are usually the bridges between groups. Lose them and the teams fall apart; close ties sit inside teams, which stay connected through each other without them.
